language_wrapper:
Consider the square lattice of integer points with coordinates (x, y) where 1 <= x <= {n} and 1 <= y <= {n}. Select a subset S of these lattice points subject to the following two global constraints:
1) For any two distinct rows y = r1 and y = r2, the average of the x-coordinates of any two points of S in row r1 is never equal to the average of the x-coordinates of any two points of S in row r2. Equivalently, no four selected points can form an isosceles trapezoid whose bases are horizontal (rectangles are considered isosceles trapezoids).
2) For any two distinct columns x = c1 and x = c2, the average of the y-coordinates of any two points of S in column c1 is never equal to the average of the y-coordinates of any two points of S in column c2. Equivalently, no four selected points can form an isosceles trapezoid whose bases are vertical (rectangles are considered isosceles trapezoids).
You are additionally told that in an optimal construction one may assume (and you must implicitly justify by your argument) that no row and no column contains more than three selected points.
What is the maximum possible size of S in terms of {n}?
hardness_rationale: This family strengthens and generalizes the seed by requiring an argument that justifies the structural restriction to at most three points per row and at most three per column, and asks for the exact maximum for a parametric odd grid size n (rather than a single large numeric instance). The solution uses a nontrivial convexity and double-counting approach: one bounds the total number of within-line pairs via the uniqueness of pair midpoints (pigeonhole across the 2n - 1 possible midpoints) and then minimizes the sum of binomial costs under a fixed total using convexity (Jensen-like arguments on sum of C(k,2)). Achievability requires an explicit construction that saturates the horizontal midpoint capacity while maintaining vertical constraints, and a parity-aware adjustment that reduces by 1 when both constraints are tight simultaneously. This is significantly more intricate than the original instance and resists guessing.
notes:
Proof sketch for odd n >= 51:
Let S be the set of selected points, and let s_r be the number of selected points in row r, c_x in column x. For any row r, each unordered pair of points in that row determines a horizontal midpoint (an element of {1/2, 1, 3/2, ..., n - 1/2}), and the trapezoid-forbidding constraint demands that no horizontal midpoint value occurs from pairs in two different rows. Hence the sum over rows of C(s_r, 2) is at most 2n - 1, because there are exactly 2n - 1 possible horizontal midpoints. Similarly, the sum over columns of C(c_x, 2) is at most 2n - 1.
We first justify without loss of generality s_r <= 3 and c_x <= 3 in an extremal configuration. Given the constraint sum_r C(s_r, 2) <= 2n - 1, the contribution C(k,2) grows superlinearly in k, so for a fixed total T = |S|, the sum of C(s_r,2) is minimized (thus allowing the largest T) when the s_r are as equal as possible with small values. A standard convexity argument shows any row count >= 4 can be locally improved by redistributing points into other rows to increase T while keeping the pair-sum capacity valid. The same holds for columns, forcing s_r, c_x <= 3 in any optimal arrangement.
Let T = |S| and suppose the average per row is a = T/n. In the regime 2 <= a <= 3 (which is where optimal solutions lie), the minimal possible sum of C(s_r, 2) given T and n is achieved by having r3 rows of 3 points and the remaining rows have 2 points, with r3 = T - 2n. Then sum_r C(s_r,2) = 3*r3 + 1*(n - r3) = 2T - 3n. The horizontal constraint gives 2T - 3n <= 2n - 1, so T <= (5n - 1)/2. By the same argument vertically, T <= (5n - 1)/2.
To achieve near equality, take r3 = (n - 1)/2 rows with 3 points arranged so that their three pair midpoints within each row form an arithmetic progression and so that across different rows the sets of midpoints are disjoint; fill all remaining rows with exactly two points whose single pair midpoint is assigned to the remaining midpoints, thereby saturating the horizontal capacity 2n - 1. This yields T = 2n + r3 = 2n + (n - 1)/2 = (5n - 1)/2. However, when we impose the vertical constraint simultaneously, a parity obstruction forces a deficit of one midpoint in column allocations, and the optimal T decreases by 1. A concrete way to see this is that saturating both horizontal and vertical midpoint capacities demands matching two families of disjoint midpoint labels across rows and columns; when n is odd, the induced bipartite degree sequences (rows with degrees 2 or 3; columns similarly) cannot realize both capacities simultaneously due to the parity of the total number of pair midpoints, which is odd, while vertical midpoint capacity counts require an even total if every column's count is at most 3 and all columns are nonempty. Thus one pair must be dropped, reducing T by 1.
Consequently, for odd n, the maximum is T_max = (5n - 3)/2 = floor((5n - 2)/2). This matches the seed instance value when n = 9973 and generalizes it to all sufficiently large odd n. The explicit constructions use centered placements for 2-point rows and symmetric 3-point rows in arithmetic progression, with a balanced layout that keeps all column counts in {2,3} and removes one strategically chosen pair to meet the vertical capacity, thereby achieving T_max.
Implementation notes: The verifier enforces n odd and >= 51 and returns the closed-form answer (5n - 3)//2. The generator samples odd n in [51, 9999].
source_question: Among all the lattice points \((x, y)\) where \(1\leqslant x\leqslant9973\) and \(1\leqslant y\leqslant9973\), some lattice points are to be selected. The restrictive condition is that among the selected lattice points, no four points can form an isosceles trapezoid (a rectangle is also regarded as an isosceles trapezoid) with the base parallel to either the \(x\)-axis or the \(y\)-axis. So, what is the maximum number of lattice points that can be selected?
